title: Directory and authorization details
rows: AD DS / AD FS
AD DS provides a directory/domain. AD FS federates authentication; it does not replace a domain controller.
Managed Microsoft AD
Managed domain controllers across two AZs; supported trusts, integrations, sharing and multi-Region replication have separate prerequisites.
AD Connector / Simple AD
Connector proxies supported requests to an existing directory. Simple AD is a limited Samba-compatible directory, with no forest trusts or MFA support.
Policy attachment
AWS-managed and customer-managed policies are reusable; inline policies belong to one identity. Inspect current AWS-managed policy versions.
ForAllValues / ForAnyValue
Compare supplied values of multivalued request keys. ForAllValues can match a missing key; use Null/presence checks and separate required-tag conditions.
STS sessions
AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithSAML, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, GetSessionToken and GetFederationToken create different session types. Trust, caller authorization and session restrictions differ.

title: Organization setup and policy boundaries
rows: Created / invited accounts
Organizations normally creates OrganizationAccountAccessRole for a created member account. Invitation does not automatically create that role.
Account moves
Meet removal prerequisites, leave/remove the old organization, then invite and accept into the new one. Recheck effective policies, service integrations and billing.
Feature modes
Consolidated billing aggregates usage/payment. All features adds governance; enabling it can require invited-account approval and cannot be downgraded to billing-only.
Discount sharing
Eligible RI/Savings Plans sharing is controlled through billing settings. It does not grant resource access or automatically share capacity reservations.
Tag policy
Supported key/value/capitalization enforcement is different from requiring every tag to exist. Use supported request-tag/provisioning controls for mandatory presence.
AI opt-out / backup policy
AI opt-out applies to eligible service data use. Backup policies express organization intent; verify assignments, successful jobs, retention and tested restores.

title: Parameter, secret and key details
rows: Parameter Store Standard
10,000 parameters per account/Region; values up to 4 KB. Standard parameters do not support advanced parameter policies or cross-account sharing.
Parameter Store Advanced
100,000 parameters per account/Region; values up to 8 KB. Supports parameter policies and supported cross-account sharing; additional charges apply. An advanced parameter cannot be downgraded.
Policies / throughput
Expiration deletes the parameter; ExpirationNotification and NoChangeNotification emit notifications. Storage tier and throughput settings are separate decisions.
Recursive paths
An allowed recursive GetParametersByPath parent can expose descendants. Design hierarchy authorization deliberately rather than treating child-path restrictions as a guaranteed boundary.
Secret rotation / CloudFormation
Dynamic references resolve during relevant stack resource operations. Changing a secret alone does not automatically refresh the resource that consumed it.
Cross-account secrets
Align the secret resource policy, caller identity permissions and customer-managed KMS key authorization.
Key custody
AWS KMS key material origin, imported material, CloudHSM custom key stores and external key stores have different custody and availability dependencies.
TLS with CloudHSM
The application server terminates TLS and uses supported HSM-backed private-key operations. CloudHSM is not a transparent traffic proxy.

title: Network controls and diagnostic precision
rows: Security groups
Stateful allow rules at supported resource/ENI scope. They do not create routes.
Network ACLs
Stateless subnet controls; numbered allow/deny rules use first match. Permit return traffic and the actual client ephemeral-port range.
Flow Log fields
Read interface, srcaddr/dstaddr, ports, protocol, counts, start/end, action and log-status. pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr can preserve original packet addresses across intermediaries.
Diagnostic limits
ACCEPT is not proof of application success; REJECT alone does not identify the complete cause. Excluded traffic, delays and SKIPDATA limit observations.
NAT instance
Configure both route directions, public connectivity, security controls and disabled source/destination checking. Operate capacity, patching and recovery yourself.
Private DNS
Verify VPC DNS settings, endpoint scope, zone conflicts and hybrid Resolver forwarding. DNS resolution, connectivity and authorization are separate checks.

title: DNS routing and health details
rows: IP-based routing
Uses configured source CIDR collections; account for recursive resolver behavior and EDNS Client Subnet support.
Geolocation / geoproximity
Geolocation uses geographic policy; geoproximity uses resource location and bias. Current geoproximity records can be managed directly; Traffic Flow is not universally mandatory.
Weighted records
Weights influence eligible DNS answers, not an exact percentage of HTTP requests. Resolver/client caching, TTLs and health affect observed traffic.
Endpoint health
HTTP/HTTPS checks evaluate supported response status and optional string matching in the first 5,120 response bytes. Route 53 global checker aggregation differs from one probe result.
Private endpoints
Public Route 53 checkers cannot directly probe arbitrary private addresses; use appropriate CloudWatch-alarm or calculated health designs.
Calculated checks

AWS documentation describes child-check limits differently across overview and console pages (255/256). Check the current API/console constraint for the operation instead of assuming interchangeability.
Traffic Flow
Policies and policy records are versioned configuration. A policy change and DNS cache expiry are separate events.

title: S3 access and legacy feature boundaries
rows: Multi-Region Access Points
A global access/routing endpoint does not automatically replicate bucket data. Configure replication and test failover independently.
Presigned URLs
They carry the signing principal's permitted operation. They expire no later than the underlying credentials and remain subject to applicable policy restrictions.
Object Lambda
Since 7 November 2025, availability is restricted to existing customers and selected APN partners. Treat older PDF designs as eligibility-dependent.
Glacier Vault Lock
A legacy Glacier vault policy lock is different from S3 Object Lock and from using an S3 Glacier storage class.
Observability
Server access logs, CloudTrail data events and CloudWatch metrics answer different questions; configuration does not prove complete event capture.

title: EBS volume limits and comparison
rows: gp3
1 GiB–64 TiB; up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s. Includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline; provisioning ratios, instance limits and platform constraints apply.
gp2
1 GiB–16 TiB; up to 16,000 IOPS and 250 MiB/s. Performance and burst behavior depend on size.
io2 Block Express
4 GiB–64 TiB; up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s on compatible instances/configurations; designed for 99.999% durability.
io1
4 GiB–16 TiB; up to 64,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s under supported instance/configuration conditions.
st1 / sc1
125 GiB–16 TiB; up to 500/250 MiB/s and 500/250 IOPS at 1 MiB I/O respectively. Throughput-oriented HDD; cannot be boot volumes.
Multi-Attach
Supported io1/io2 volumes: up to 16 Nitro instances in one AZ. Linux supports io1/io2; Windows supports io2. Coordinate concurrent writes with a suitable application/filesystem.
Scope exceptions
Outposts gp3 limits differ from regional gp3. The PDF's 7.5/60 TiB instance-store examples describe particular instance configurations, not a universal current limit.
Instance store lifecycle
Host-local block storage survives a normal reboot, but data is lost on stop/termination and can be lost on host failure. Capacity cannot be expanded like EBS; operate independent backups.

title: Snapshot recovery and EFS details
rows: Capture consistency
Detachment is optional. Quiesce the application and flush pending writes; coordinate related volumes. A crash-consistent block capture is not automatically application-consistent.
Fast Snapshot Restore

Enable per snapshot/AZ and account for additional charges and volume-creation credits. Snapshot size is limited to 16 TiB; full performance benefits have documented 64,000 IOPS / 1,000 MiB/s boundaries.
Provisioned initialization
Choose 100–300 MiB/s where supported. Initialization concerns snapshot data size, not simply allocated volume size. Specifying a rate takes precedence over FSR.
Manual initialization
Read every required block safely using a supported read-only method such as fio/dd to /dev/null. Do not overwrite the restored device.
EFS bursting
Baseline is 50 MiB/s per TiB of Standard storage, with a minimum baseline. Burst credits and capacity determine burst performance; read requests are metered at one-third the write rate.
EFS access controls
Network reachability, IAM client permissions and POSIX permissions are separate gates. Access points can enforce a root directory and UID/GID; they do not bypass missing permissions.
Default EFS policy
Without a user-configured filesystem policy, the default allows anonymous network-reachable clients, subject to POSIX permissions. Use the mount helper and supported IAM authorization deliberately.
EFS replication
Initial synchronization precedes destination availability. Most filesystems target a 15-minute RPO; high-churn very large filesystems/files can exceed it. Monitor TimeSinceLastSync and test RTO.
Current performance
Regional Elastic throughput limits vary by Region and supported client. Older universal ceilings in the PDF are historical; check the current performance table for the selected configuration.
EFS protocol and scale
Managed NFSv4.0/v4.1 with POSIX semantics; scalable to petabytes and thousands of concurrent clients. Linux file workloads differ from native Windows SMB.
Performance modes
General Purpose is recommended for low latency. Max I/O is a creation-time choice, has higher per-operation latency, and is unavailable for One Zone filesystems or Elastic throughput.
Storage class eligibility

Regional supports Standard, IA and Archive; One Zone supports One Zone and One Zone-IA, with automatic backups enabled by default. Archive requires supported Regional/Elastic configuration. Lifecycle eligibility and minimum storage charges apply.
Hybrid mount paths
Use supported private DX/VPN or peering paths, NFS TCP 2049, mount-target security groups and correct DNS or explicit target addressing. Design redundant connectivity and mount targets.
Cost comparisons

The PDF’s 3× gp2, 50% Archive and >90% savings figures are scenario/price illustrations, not universal current prices. Compare Region-specific storage, access, retrieval, throughput and minimum-duration charges.
Replication throughput
Replication uses managed capacity rather than consuming the source filesystem’s provisioned throughput allocation. This does not eliminate initial-copy duration, lag or failover work.

title: FSx and Storage Gateway details
rows: FSx for Windows
SMB/NTFS, AD authentication, ACLs, quotas and supported DFS patterns. Distinguish SSD/HDD, backup protection and Single-AZ/Multi-AZ availability.
Lustre scratch
Data is not replicated; failed file servers are not replaced. Scratch can burst up to six times a 200 MBps/TiB baseline. Keep recreatable inputs and valuable outputs independently protected.
Lustre persistent SSD/HDD
Replicates data within one AZ and replaces failed servers. Persistent 1/2 and media choices have different capacity, throughput and deployment constraints.
Lustre Intelligent-Tiering

Current persistent Intelligent-Tiering replicates data across multiple AZs, offers elastic tiered storage and optional SSD read cache. Data durability is distinct from serving availability and application DR.
ONTAP / OpenZFS
ONTAP supports NFS/SMB/iSCSI and storage-management features. OpenZFS serves NFS; do not treat older headline IOPS/latency figures as guarantees for every configuration.
File Gateway disks
S3 File Gateway uses local cache disks. Volume/Tape Gateway upload buffers are separate type-specific concepts; do not apply their disk model to File Gateway.
S3 event workflows
Newly uploaded objects can trigger supported event processing and feed Athena, Redshift Spectrum or EMR. Configure replication separately for a second Region.
Multiple gateways
Prefer one authoritative writer per object set with read-only consumers where appropriate. RefreshCache updates inventory; it does not eagerly download all object bytes.
Recovery and immutability

Lifecycle can reduce storage cost but archive retrieval may require restoration. Recover a previous version deliberately, refresh gateway metadata, and understand Object Lock protects object versions rather than freezing every filename forever.
Volume / Tape Gateway
Volume Gateway recovery uses EBS snapshots with type-specific local storage. Tape Gateway eject/archive and virtual-library recovery are different workflows.
Legacy availability

Storage Gateway hardware appliances stopped new sales in May 2025, with existing support scheduled through May 2028. FSx File Gateway is unavailable to new customers; retain historical context without recommending an ineligible new deployment.
Supported client examples

ONTAP and OpenZFS can serve compatible Linux, Windows and macOS clients, on-premises systems, EC2 and container workloads. VMware, WorkSpaces and application-streaming integrations require supported protocol/client/network configurations.
Gateway deployment

Use a supported VM/host deployment and type-specific CPU, memory, disk and network sizing. The PDF’s hardware-purchase path is historical; private or encrypted internet transport remains a separate design choice.
S3 File Gateway storage classes

Supported active-object destinations include Standard, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Intelligent-Tiering. Lifecycle transitions into archive classes change retrieval behavior; confirm current gateway compatibility and restore requirements.
FSx File Gateway historical architecture
The historical service exposed FSx for Windows via SMB with NTFS/AD compatibility and a local hot-data cache, commonly for home directories/group shares. It is closed to new customers.
Lustre repository behavior

Import namespace/metadata and load needed file contents on demand. Retained data can avoid repeated reads, but eviction and configured import/export behavior determine later S3 requests. Supported private connectivity is required for on-premises clients.

title: RDS deployment, security and recovery
rows: Classic Multi-AZ instance
Synchronous standby provides availability and automatic endpoint failover. The standby does not serve reads. Read replicas are asynchronous and may require explicit promotion.
Multi-AZ DB cluster
Supported MySQL/PostgreSQL deployments use a writer and two readable replicas across three AZs with semisynchronous replication. This differs from the classic non-readable standby.
Private connection path
Validate subnet routing, DNS, security groups, supported port and database grants. Lambda needs supported private reachability to the database or proxy.
Backups and snapshots

Automated backups enable point-in-time recovery within the configured retention window, up to 35 days. A standard RDS DB instance supports 0–35 days (0 disables automated backups); a Multi-AZ DB cluster requires 1–35 days. Defaults depend on the creation interface. Manual snapshots persist until deleted. Restore creates another database endpoint. Check encryption keys, engine compatibility and application consistency.
Regional recovery

Copy eligible snapshots or use eligible cross-Region asynchronous replicas. Detect failure, fence the former writer, promote deliberately, validate data and cut over application endpoints. DNS changes alone do not promote a database.
Encryption layers
KMS protects eligible storage, backups and snapshots. TLS protects the connection. Oracle/SQL Server TDE depends on engine/edition support; it is not interchangeable with network encryption.
Encrypt existing data
Use a supported encrypted snapshot-copy and restore workflow; verify KMS policies and grants before cutover. Changing a connection setting does not encrypt an old volume.
IAM login

Supported MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL configurations accept a signed login token valid for 15 minutes. Caller rds-db:connect permission, database-user setup/grants and TLS remain required. Token expiry does not terminate an authenticated session.
Proxy constraints

RDS Proxy uses private endpoints and supported database targets. Validate VPC connectivity, authentication and capacity. Session pinning reduces connection multiplexing; a proxy does not create unlimited database capacity.
Read-only proxy endpoint
An additional read-only proxy endpoint can target eligible Aurora readers. It is not a generic endpoint for arbitrary ordinary RDS read replicas.
Oracle RMAN boundary

Supported rdsadmin packages can produce RMAN backups for export and self-managed restoration. You cannot restore an arbitrary RMAN backup directly into managed RDS. Standard RDS Oracle does not provide RAC.
MySQL migration

Export a consistent logical seed to a compatible external EC2/on-premises target, catch up replication where supported, stop/fence writes and test a controlled cutover. DMS has separate source/target and logging prerequisites.
Audit evidence

CloudTrail records supported control-plane API actions, not every SQL statement. Use supported engine audit/general/slow/error logs for database evidence. RDS events through SNS complement CloudWatch metrics and query diagnosis.

title: Aurora topology and operational exceptions
rows: Storage versus compute

Six storage copies across three AZs are separate from writer/reader compute instances. Classic storage-quorum concepts use four of six for writes and three of six for reads, with self-healing distributed storage.
Current storage capacity

Eligible Aurora PostgreSQL 17.5+, 16.9+, 15.13+ and Aurora MySQL 3.10+ configurations support up to 256 TiB; older supported configurations can retain a 128-TiB maximum. Confirm engine/version eligibility.
Reader count and balancing

An ordinary Aurora cluster supports up to 15 reader replicas. The reader endpoint balances new connections rather than individual SQL queries. With no reader, it connects to the writer and can accept writes.
Endpoint identity

The writer endpoint follows the primary. Reader endpoints serve eligible reader connections; instance endpoints select a particular instance for diagnosis. Reconnect after failover and account for DNS/client connection caching.
Custom endpoint membership

ANY versus READER types and static/exclusion membership affect routing. Console-created custom endpoints use ANY. A selected analytical subset does not remove those instances from the built-in reader endpoint. Custom endpoints are not restored from snapshots.
Scaling controls

Storage grows independently from compute. Reader Auto Scaling changes eligible reader count within configured bounds, not the writer size. Serverless v2 scales supported ACUs within configured minimum/maximum bounds.
Serverless eligibility and costs

Zero-ACU auto-pause requires supported versions/configurations and idle conditions. Capacity billing does not eliminate storage, I/O, backup or transfer charges. The old Serverless v1 proxy-fleet illustration is not the v2 architecture.
Data API

Supported provisioned and Serverless Aurora configurations can execute SQL through HTTPS. Validate engine/Region eligibility, Data API IAM authorization, Secrets Manager access, applicable KMS permissions and database grants. Credentials remain necessary behind the interface.
Global topology

Current eligible configurations allow up to 10 secondary Regions. Primary readers plus secondary clusters must not exceed 15; a secondary cluster supports up to 16 instances. Replication is asynchronous and applies database storage changes, not arbitrary selected tables.
Global recovery

A planned synchronized switchover avoids data loss; unplanned failover can lose recent unreplicated changes. Measure lag, RPO, RTO and application reconnection. Supported Aurora PostgreSQL rds.global_db_rpo controls can block commits when all secondaries exceed the target lag.
Write forwarding

A secondary forwards eligible writes to the primary, which commits before changes replicate back. Forwarding does not create independent regional writers or eliminate network latency and consistency restrictions.
Diagnosis

Use current CloudWatch Database Insights console workflows for database load/waits and SQL/host/user dimensions, CloudWatch CPU/memory/swap metrics, Enhanced Monitoring host/process detail and engine slow-query evidence. Historical Performance Insights references require the current console/API distinction.
S3 integration

Aurora MySQL LOAD DATA FROM S3 and SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3 need supported versions, cluster IAM-role configuration and bucket/KMS access. Aurora PostgreSQL aws_s3 import/export functions need extension setup, permissions and supported data formats. These are engine-specific operations, not arbitrary S3 filesystem access.
Migration

Use an eligible RDS snapshot restore or supported Aurora read-replica migration/promotion path. Validate source version, extensions, parameters, client behavior, reconciliation, rollback and cutover before production traffic.

title: DynamoDB exact limits and consistency
rows: Item model

Maximum item size is 400 KB including attribute names and values. Scalar types include String, Number, Binary, Boolean and Null; documents use List/Map; sets use String/Number/Binary. The Cassandra analogy does not imply compatible APIs.
Primary keys

A partition-only key uniquely identifies an item. With a composite key, the partition-plus-sort-key pair is unique; related items can share a partition key. Diverse workload keys help distribute load.
Query versus Scan

Query requires partition-key equality and supports optional sort-key conditions. Scan reads across items. Filter expressions are applied after reads and do not erase the read capacity already consumed; paginate results.
LSI

Same partition key, alternate sort key; create only with the table. Up to five per table, 10-GB item-collection limit per partition-key value, shared table capacity. Supported LSI reads can request strong consistency.
GSI

An alternate partition/sort key can be added later. Default quota is 20 per table, subject to approved increases. A GSI has separate provisioned capacity when that mode applies and supports eventual consistency only. Projections affect available attributes and cost.
Capacity mode

Provisioned mode allocates capacity and can use configured Auto Scaling; on-demand mode charges for requests and adapts within supported limits. Neither design removes throttling, hot-partition risks or account/table quotas.
Read units

For an individual read, round item size up to 4-KB units: strong = one unit, eventual = half a unit, transactional = two units. An 8-KB item needs 2, 1 or 4 units respectively. Batch/Query aggregation rules require the operation-specific calculation.
Write units

For an individual standard write, round size up to 1-KB units; transactional writes use twice the units. A 2-KB item needs 2 standard or 4 transactional write units. Updates/deletes have their own charged-size rules.
Consistency scope

Regional table and supported LSI reads may use strong consistency; GSIs remain eventual. A strongly consistent read of an MREC regional replica does not guarantee the latest write made in another Region.
Transactions

Up to 100 distinct items/actions and 4 MB per transaction, within one account and Region. Conditional writes protect an individual precondition; multi-item transactions provide a different atomicity boundary.
TTL
Use a numeric Unix-epoch timestamp in seconds. Removal is asynchronous and expired items can remain visible; enforce authorization/session expiry in application logic. TTL is not an exact scheduler.
Streams versus Kinesis

Native Streams retains records for 24 hours with per-item order. Consumer retries can repeat processing even though native stream records themselves are not duplicated. Kinesis capture offers configured 24-hour to 365-day retention, but can deliver duplicates and changes out of order; checkpoint, deduplicate and reconcile.
MREC

Multi-Region eventual consistency supports regional writes with asynchronous replication and conflict resolution. It uses Streams. The application selects suitable regional endpoints and handles failures; Route 53 does not automatically route DynamoDB SDK table operations.
MRSC

Multi-Region strong consistency uses supported three-Region groups, with either three replicas or two replicas plus a non-client-serving witness. It does not require Streams. TTL, LSIs and transactions are not supported; GSIs remain eventual.
Table classes and backups

Standard offers lower request cost and higher storage cost than Standard-IA. Both remain online; Standard-IA is not archive storage. On-demand backups and point-in-time recovery solve recovery history, independently of table class. DynamoDB PITR supports a configured 1–35-day window, default 35 days, with per-second recovery points; restore creates a new table.
S3 metadata index

Store queryable object metadata in DynamoDB; the object remains in S3. Process supported object events reliably and reconcile missed/duplicate/out-of-order updates. Storage totals require maintained aggregates, not a free sum over all objects.

title: DAX and ElastiCache decisions
rows: DAX topology

DynamoDB Accelerator is a managed regional DynamoDB cache requiring a DAX-aware client. Maximum cluster size is 11 nodes: one primary and up to 10 replicas. At least three nodes across AZs is the production availability recommendation; the source PDF ten-total limit is obsolete.
DAX request paths

Hits return from DAX. Misses read DynamoDB and populate the cache. Writes through DAX go to DynamoDB and update applicable item-cache entries. Strong and transactional reads pass through without populating the cache.
DAX freshness

Default TTL is five minutes with separately controlled item and query caches. Updating an item does not invalidate cached Query/Scan results. Direct-table or cross-Region updates can bypass a local cache; eventual reads may remain stale until expiry/refresh.
DAX security

Deploy with supported private VPC connectivity and security groups, IAM authorization, at-rest KMS encryption and supported audit controls. DAX does not solve every write-heavy or hot-partition workload.
Cache contract

DAX understands supported DynamoDB operations. ElastiCache stores application-selected values such as computed aggregates or sessions; the application owns keys, serialization, invalidation and fallback behavior.
Cache-aside

The application checks the cache. On a miss it reads the database and fills the cache. The cache does not independently query an arbitrary RDS database. Test expiry, stampedes, outages, eviction and source load.
Write/invalidation order

Write the authoritative store, then perform a selected update/invalidation strategy with race/retry handling. TTL bounds retained data age but does not guarantee immediate freshness. Session authorization must check its actual expiry.
Engine/deployment differences

Valkey/Redis OSS replication and automatic failover differ from sharding for capacity. Replica reads may lag. Memcached multithreading and horizontal distribution do not imply the same persistence/failover contract.
Persistence exception

Managed ElastiCache Valkey/Redis OSS does not provide generic self-managed AOF configuration. Node-based Memcached has no snapshot backup; Serverless Memcached supports snapshots. Validate engine, deployment and current feature support separately.
Extreme-rate bottlenecks

Measure client, DNS, edge, API throttling, Lambda concurrency, network, database partitions, cache misses and cost as one path. The PDF historic node capacities, API/Lambda/edge defaults and unbounded queue claims are not current universal guarantees. S3 baseline is 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix, not the PDF 5,550 typo; KMS can impose another quota. Detailed quotas belong to Modules 07/09 and later Modules 13–16.
Valkey optional durability

Eligible node-based ElastiCache for Valkey supports optional Multi-AZ transactional-log durability. Synchronous mode persists before acknowledging and adds write latency; asynchronous mode acknowledges first and can lose up to 10 seconds of uncommitted writes during failure. Durability is configuration-specific and is not generic Redis AOF. Compare this selected contract with MemoryDB rather than assuming all ElastiCache data is disposable.
Serverless public endpoint exception

Eligible ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey 9.0+ supports a public connection option requiring IAM authentication and TLS 1.3. VPC/private designs remain separate choices; validate engine, version, connection type and authorization rather than describing every ElastiCache deployment as VPC-only.

title: Search, documents and time-series boundaries
rows: OpenSearch modes

Managed domains and Serverless collections have different scaling and operational contracts. Serverless encryption/network/data-access policies and identity authorization are separate controls. OpenSearch is a derived search index, not a drop-in relational source of truth.
Pipeline roles

Logstash or supported ingestion components transform/deliver data; OpenSearch indexes and searches it; Dashboards visualizes results. Retention and granularity depend on configuration, not a universal advantage over CloudWatch.
DynamoDB search index

Source CRUD operations remain in DynamoDB. A supported Streams/Lambda or ingestion pipeline maintains the search view asynchronously. Handle initial backfill, updates, deletions, duplicates, retries and reconciliation; search is not immediately authoritative.
CloudWatch delivery

Supported subscription/Lambda paths prioritize low-latency processing. Amazon Data Firehose buffers and delivers supported destinations. Validate destination compatibility, retry/rejected records and latency rather than assuming identical real-time behavior.
DocumentDB compatibility

A managed document database with supported MongoDB-compatible APIs is not the identical MongoDB engine. Validate operators, drivers, indexes, transactions and workload behavior. Instance-based storage grows in 10-GB increments; eligible engine 8+ supports 256 TiB, earlier configurations 128 TiB; up to 15 readers.
DocumentDB pricing

On-demand instance compute is billed per second with a ten-minute minimum. Standard charges supported I/O separately; I/O-Optimized changes the storage/I/O pricing model. Include reader instances, storage, backups, transfer and Region-specific prices; benchmark rather than asserting a universal throughput gain.
LiveAnalytics availability

Timestream for LiveAnalytics stopped accepting new customers on 20 June 2025. Existing-service memory/magnetic tiering, SQL, scheduled queries, multi-measure records, time-series functions and encryption remain teaching concepts. Evaluate current Timestream for InfluxDB independently; APIs, connectors and tiering are not interchangeable.
Time-series pipeline

Validate producer write formats, event time, late arrivals, retention, duplicates and retries. Supported IoT/Kinesis/Lambda/Flink, SQL/JDBC/BI/ML integrations depend on the chosen product. Historic marketing speed/price ratios are not architecture guarantees.

title: Container runtime, ECS networking and identity
rows: Platform portability
Image OS family, CPU architecture, runtime and kernel requirements must match. Containers share host resources; their writable layer is not a durable shared database.
ECS objects

Cluster: logical grouping, including eligible Fargate capacity. Task definition: versioned configuration. Task: running one or more containers. Service: maintains desired tasks. A Reserved Instance is a billing/capacity arrangement, not an ECS launch type.
Roles

Task role authorizes application AWS API access. Execution role authorizes supported agent startup operations such as ECR pulls, awslogs and secret retrieval. EC2 instance profile supports the host/agent. Scope trust, actions, resources and applicable KMS access to the actual caller.
Bridge and host

On Linux EC2, bridge supports dynamic host-port mapping. Host mode shares the host network, so the same host port cannot be reused by competing copies. An ALB target for bridge uses the instance and registered host port.
awsvpc and none

awsvpc supplies a task ENI/private IP and security groups; Fargate requires it. Use IP target groups for supported awsvpc service load balancing. None provides no external task networking or port mappings. Windows mode support differs.
Fargate private startup

Provide subnet IP capacity and required IAM/network paths. ECR image pull commonly needs ECR API and registry interface endpoints plus an S3 gateway endpoint for layers; CloudWatch Logs and Secrets Manager need their own access. NAT is another appropriate egress option.
Secret refresh

Environment references are resolved at task start. Rotation does not update a running process environment; redeploy tasks or implement supported application retrieval/caching. Do not expose secrets in image layers, logs or broad diagnostic access.
Health and replacement

Configure the application port, health-check path, security-group source and target type. Rolling updates need sufficient healthy capacity and deployment settings. Several tasks on one EC2 host share its failure boundary.
Task versus host scaling

Application Auto Scaling changes desired service tasks with target tracking, step or scheduled policies. EC2 capacity-provider/ASG scaling supplies eligible slots. CPU, memory, ENIs, subnet IPs, quotas and placement constraints can each block placement.
Spot strategy

Only one capacity provider in a strategy can have a base. Base is fulfilled first; weights distribute subsequent placements. FARGATE_SPOT can be interrupted or unavailable; it does not automatically fall back to FARGATE. Plan graceful stop, replicas and checkpointing.
Managed Instances

Current ECS Managed Instances adds a managed compute option with its own supported task/network settings. Confirm current migration and capacity-provider compatibility instead of generalizing old EC2/Fargate-only statements.
Predictive service scaling

Current ECS predictive scaling adds forecast-based service task scale-out alongside target tracking, step and scheduled scaling. It requires at least 24 hours of historical load data; evaluate forecast-only mode before enabling forecast-and-scale. It does not scale in tasks by itself: combine appropriate dynamic scaling. A forecast can analyze up to 14 days, project hourly needs for 48 hours and refresh every six hours. Capacity limits and optional automatic maximum increases need cost/guardrail review; host capacity remains a separate loop.

title: Image registry, scanning and regional distribution
rows: Image identity
A tag is a reference; the digest identifies content. Use reproducible build inputs and record the digest deployed. Appropriate tag-immutability settings reduce accidental release changes.
Repository access

Authentication is separate from permission to pull/push. Cross-account pulls need applicable identity and repository policy authorization; registry token acquisition alone is insufficient. Image network reachability remains required.
Lifecycle preview

Preview retention rules, preserve deployed and rollback images, and account for manifest lists/reference artifacts. An image still running from a local cache may later fail to redeploy if its registry content was removed.
Cross-account replication

Source registry rules specify destinations. Destination registry permissions grant ecr:ReplicateImage and, for automatic repository creation, ecr:CreateRepository. Without creation permission, precreate matching destination repositories.
Replication completeness

Automatic replication does not simply synchronize every historical image and deletion. Validate eligible push/restore triggers and use supported replication backfill deliberately. Destination settings, policies, lifecycle and deployment remain separate; verify destination digest and status.
Basic scanning

Current ECR Basic Scanning uses AWS-native OS vulnerability detection, with supported manual/on-push operation. Retrieve current findings through supported APIs; old DescribeImages summary/status fields are not the current findings interface.
Enhanced scanning

Inspector covers supported OS and programming-language packages, configured repository filters and rescan rules. Current eligibility/history and rescan-duration settings matter; enabling scanning does not guarantee every old image was assessed.
Events and remediation

Basic and enhanced scan events have different producers/details. Process supported EventBridge events, prioritize exploitable findings, rebuild and scan a patched image, then deploy the new digest. Scanning itself does not patch or universally block deployment.

title: Kubernetes compute, storage and tenant boundaries
rows: Control plane and Region

EKS manages a regional Kubernetes control plane. Deploy separate clusters for regional recovery; restore workload definitions, image availability, secrets, state and routing. Kubernetes API portability does not remove cloud-specific integrations. The EKS management API PrivateLink endpoint does not carry Kubernetes API traffic; configure the separate cluster API endpoint and private access path.
Compute ownership

Managed node groups automate supported EC2/ASG lifecycle operations; self-managed nodes require more bootstrap and patching ownership, including compatible optimized AMIs. EKS Auto Mode manages additional supported compute/platform functions. Verify workload and platform support.
Fargate restrictions

EKS Fargate has no Fargate Spot and does not support arbitrary DaemonSets, privileged patterns or EBS-backed Pod volumes. Select compatible storage and identity rather than assuming ECS Fargate feature parity.
Cluster and workload authorization

EKS access entries/configuration and Kubernetes RBAC authorize cluster actions. IRSA or supported EKS Pod Identity authorizes workload AWS API calls. IRSA requires the cluster IAM OIDC provider and a trust policy scoped to the expected service-account subject and STS audience. Pod Identity uses its supported association and agent path and is not supported on Fargate; restrict IMDS and avoid broad node-role inheritance.
PVC/PV and provisioning

StorageClass describes dynamic-provisioning parameters through a compatible provisioner; statically provisioned volumes are also valid. Match access mode, topology, reclaim policy, driver identity, filesystem/network permissions and backup/restore.
EBS and EFS

EBS data volumes are AZ-scoped; compatible scheduling must follow volume topology. EFS supports shared access. EKS Fargate supports eligible EFS static provisioning and does not support dynamic persistent-volume provisioning for Fargate workloads.
FSx drivers

FSx for Lustre uses supported CSI components and compatible nodes; ONTAP integrations such as Trident have different protocols and provisioning contracts. FSx for Lustre CSI is not supported on Fargate. The current ONTAP CSI integration is not compatible with EKS Hybrid Nodes; validate the selected driver and compute. This list does not promise universal backend support.
Soft tenancy

Namespaces, scoped RBAC, quotas, admission restrictions and workload identities support pooled isolation. A namespace by itself is not a security boundary; separate cluster/account choices can reduce trust and blast-radius exposure.
Network enforcement

Start with default-deny intent and explicit required DNS/dependency paths, using a supported enforcing network-policy implementation. Shared nodes share kernel risks; combine traffic controls with data authorization, metadata restrictions and resource limits.
Tenant context

Derive tenant identity from authenticated trusted context and enforce it in every data access path. Silo dedicates resources, pool shares them with isolation controls, and bridge combines models. Test cross-tenant reads/writes, not only network reachability.

title: Service discovery, mesh and cross-account connectivity
rows: Cloud Map data path

Register endpoint identity/attributes/health and use eligible API or DNS discovery. The caller connects directly to the discovered backend; Cloud Map is not an inline load balancer or a network tunnel.
Health and caching

DiscoverInstances supports HEALTHY, UNHEALTHY, ALL and HEALTHY_OR_ELSE_ALL filtering. Without configured health checks, filtering may not exclude instances. DNS routing/fail-open behavior and TTL/client caches differ; do not assume instant removal or an authorization boundary.
Service Connect scope

Each service joins one namespace; compatible participating services can span ECS clusters in the same Region and supported shared namespaces/accounts. They still need routes and security-group reachability. Outside clients need another discovery/interconnection method.
Service Connect TLS

Supported TLS configuration uses AWS Private CA and an ECS infrastructure role, with managed certificate secrets/rotation. Configure required permissions and protect those secrets. Encryption/rotation behavior does not automatically supply all tenant authorization or legacy mesh features.
App Mesh disposition

Support ended 30 September 2026 and resources are no longer available as a current choice. Preserve mesh concepts and evaluate supported Service Connect, Lattice or Kubernetes options against explicit telemetry, TLS, retries and traffic-control requirements.
Lattice controls

Service networks, VPC associations, listeners, target groups and supported sharing provide connectivity. IAM-auth policies and caller IAM authorization are distinct controls; signed requests are required when using IAM authentication. Verify target health, security paths and logs.
Isolation validation

Use an allow/deny matrix across application authorization, IAM and network policies. A timeout may indicate DNS or routing failure rather than an enforced tenant boundary. Preserve policy versions and negative-test evidence.

title: App Runner and hybrid operating-model exceptions
rows: Current eligibility

App Runner closed to new customers on 31 March 2026. Existing eligible customers can continue creating/using services, with continued security/availability investment but no planned new features. Retain code/image, deployment, health, scaling, HTTPS and encryption concepts as historical/current-existing-customer knowledge.
Migration candidate

AWS recommends evaluating ECS Express Mode, which creates a Fargate service, ALB, scaling and networking in the account using an image and required IAM roles. It has no separate Express Mode charge; underlying resources remain billable. Validate ownership, private dependencies and deployment parity.
Ingress versus egress

An App Runner VPC connector controls application outbound private-network traffic. It does not make incoming traffic private. Private ingress uses supported VPC interface endpoint and ingress-connection configuration; VPC egress may require NAT or endpoints for public dependencies.
Regional example correction

Use independent supported regional services and validated custom-domain, certificate and routing configurations. A hostname is not a literal A-record IP value. Image replication, global-table data replication and traffic failover have separate configuration and verification.
ECS Anywhere

Register supported external hosts with ECS/SSM agents, IAM and EXTERNAL launch type. Management depends on regional connectivity, while already-running tasks may continue during disconnection. External networking supports bridge/host/none, not awsvpc; service load balancing/discovery are not supported.
Hybrid host support

Current ECS Anywhere operating-system support changed in August 2026. Validate the current supported list rather than using an old host image. Customer-owned infrastructure, patching, capacity, local access and recovery remain operational responsibilities.
EKS Anywhere correction

A customer-operated local Kubernetes control plane can run connected, disconnected or air-gapped using prepared dependencies/mirrors. Optional EKS Connector provides console visibility; it does not make the local control plane a managed regional EKS cluster. Full disconnection does not require abandoning EKS Anywhere for bare EKS Distro.

title: Lambda execution, runtime and package precision
rows: Memory and CPU

Standard Event Functions configure 128–10,240 MB in 1-MB increments; CPU scales with memory. At 1,769 MB the allocation is equivalent to one vCPU, correcting the source two-vCPU claim. Supported maximum-memory configurations can reach six vCPUs; profile single-threaded versus parallel code.
Timeout scope

Standard maximum invocation timeout is 900 seconds; default is 3 seconds. Eligible Managed Instances async/event-source-mapping invocations can use 5,400 seconds, except Amazon MQ/DocumentDB sources. Workflow wall-clock duration and individual invocation duration differ.
Temporary storage

/tmp can be 512–10,240 MB in 1-MB increments for supported standard configurations; it is temporary, separate from memory and not durable state. Reuse does not guarantee retention across environments.
ZIP and layers

Direct uploaded ZIP packages:50 MB compressed; uncompressed function plus included layers:250 MB. Supported larger compressed artifacts can use S3 upload. Up to five layers. Container images use a different package contract.
Container deployment

Up to 10 GB uncompressed including image layers. Match supported architecture/OS and implement Lambda Runtime API; read-only root filesystem with supported /tmp writes. Patch the image and validate ECR access; arbitrary Docker server images are not automatically compatible.
Environment and policy sizes
Aggregate environment variables:4 KB. Function resource-based policy:20 KB. These do not replace Secrets Manager or least-privilege application/configuration design.
Buffered and async payloads

Synchronous buffered request/response:6 MB each. Async invocation payload:1 MB, replacing the PDF256 KB value. Base 64 encoding and integration envelopes can enlarge data; the smallest boundary in the path wins.
Response streaming

Lambda synchronous streamed responses support up to 200 MB; after the first 6 MB, the remaining Lambda stream is limited to 2 MB/s. Downstream API/CloudFront/client constraints are separate. Streaming responses do not imply streaming requests.
Runtime lifecycle

Node.js, Python, Java, .NET and Ruby support is versioned. PowerShell/custom languages require compatible supported packaging/runtime integration, not an assumed permanent managed-runtime entitlement. Track deprecation, OS libraries and SDK versions.
Current function models

Standard Event Functions are the course baseline. Lambda Managed Instances, durable functions, Web Functions and MicroVM offerings have distinct compute/API/availability/quota contracts. Check the chosen model; do not generalize standard per-environment or duration rules to all Lambda offerings.

title: Lambda concurrency, retries and failure retention
rows: Account and function scaling

Typical regional account concurrency default:1,000; newer accounts can start lower, with increases subject to approval. Standard per-function environment scale-out limit:1,000 environments per 10 seconds. Request rate, source concurrency and downstream limits remain separate.
Reserved versus provisioned

Reserved concurrency allocates an exclusive share and an upper bound without pre-initializing. Provisioned concurrency keeps qualified version/alias environments ready and adds cost. Leave required unreserved capacity: with the normal quota,100 units remain for unreserved functions. Reserved zero intentionally stops processing; async failure-retention behavior needs review.
Capacity sizing
Approximate steady concurrency=RPS×average duration in seconds.200 RPS×0.5s≈100concurrent. Tail latency, spikes, initialization and retries need headroom; this arithmetic is not a burst guarantee.
SnapStart support

Current supported Java 11+, Python 3.12+ and .NET8+ runtime configurations and corresponding eligible container formats must be checked against the current list. Published versions/aliases only, not$LATEST. No provisioned concurrency, EFS or /tmp>512 MB; restore uniqueness and network reconnection must be validated.
Synchronous retries

Caller/integration decides supported retry behavior. Check function/application errors even when the invoke transport succeeds. A caller timeout can occur after a side effect commits; use idempotency keys and a reconciliation/query path.
Asynchronous function errors

Default code/runtime error behavior: initial attempt plus two retries, ordinarily about 1minute then 2 minutes later. Configure maximum retry attempts 0–2 and maximum event age 60–21,600 seconds where supported. This is not the universal retry count for throttles/system failures.
Throttles and async queue age

Throttling/system errors are retried with increasing delay for up to six hours by default. Duplicates can occur even without a function error; queue pressure can age out events. Monitor age, dropped events and failure retention.
DLQ versus destination

Function DLQ: standard SNS/SQS event payload plus relevant attributes. Async destinations: request/response invocation record for success/failure using supported standard SNS/SQS, Lambda or EventBridge; S3 is failure-only. SNS256 KB can be too small for a large invocation record.
Failure-delivery permissions

Grant relevant SendMessage, Publish, PutEvents, InvokeFunction or S3 write/list permissions and required KMS access. Monitor DestinationDeliveryFailures and dead-letter errors. Unsupported FIFO destination configuration or size denial is not a successful archive.
Poller contract

SQS/Kinesis/DynamoDB event source mappings poll and batch; they do not use the function async queue retry contract. Configure source-specific failure behavior, checkpoints, concurrency and partial-batch handling. SQS visibility should cover processing/retry needs; successful records must not be blindly repeated.
Integration catalog

Supported API/ALB/SDK synchronous invokes; S3/SNS/EventBridge async invokes; SQS/stream polling; IoT rule, Cognito trigger and Logs subscription invocation each have distinct event, permission, timing and retry contracts. Verify the selected source rather than applying a generic Lambda rule.
IoT and Logs source contracts

AWS IoT rules invoke Lambda asynchronously and need a source-scoped function resource permission. CloudWatch Logs subscription data uses the supported awslogs.data Base64/GZIP envelope; filter and decode it correctly, avoid log-trigger recursion and validate delivery/processing failure behavior.
Cognito user-pool trigger exception

Most user-pool triggers are synchronous and require a response within a fixed five-second window; eligible retry behavior is trigger/error-specific, not a generic async Lambda rule. Asynchronous custom-sender exceptions must be checked separately. Do not confuse these triggers with legacy Cognito Sync events.

title: Lambda release, network and operational boundaries
rows: CodeDeploy modes

Examples include Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes, Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes, Canary10Percent5Minutes, Canary10Percent30Minutes and AllAtOnce. Validate supported deployment configuration, hooks, alarms and rollback; custom values require supported configuration. SAM can define deployment preferences.
Versions and alias scope

Published code and most version configuration are immutable; operational trigger/destination/provisioned-concurrency settings can still change, and supported automatic runtime patching has its own policy. An alias is a qualified pointer with supported version weighting and compatibility prerequisites. Scope invoke permissions to the actual version/alias ARN. API deployment stages are independent selectors.
Private networking

Every function runs in Lambda service-managed infrastructure; customer-VPC configuration provides Hyperplane-ENI connectivity. Select compatible subnets/security groups, ENI management permissions, DNS, route/address capacity and resource authorization.
Internet and fixed egress

Public subnet attachment gives no Lambda public IP. For standard IPv4 internet egress, use a private subnet route through an appropriately placed public NAT gateway/EIP and IGW. Consider AZ failure, cross-AZ charges, port/capacity and all egress IPs on the external allowlist.
AWS endpoints versus default log delivery

A supported DynamoDB/S3 endpoint can supply that service path; other SDK/service calls need their own endpoint or internet connectivity. Standard Lambda service delivery of execution logs is not evidence that application SDK HTTPS calls can reach CloudWatch or another service without a network path.
Logging and tracing permission

For standard CloudWatch Logs delivery, scope supported logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents permissions appropriately. Supported active tracing can require xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords. Protect sensitive values and set retention; API Gateway tracing and downstream application spans remain separate.
X-Ray tooling timeline

X-Ray SDKs and daemon entered maintenance 25 February 2026; support ends 25 February 2027 per current timeline. AWS recommends OpenTelemetry-compatible instrumentation. X-Ray service tracing is not declared retired by the SDK timeline.
Thumbnail and scheduled jobs

Filter source notifications to avoid output recursion; use deterministic output/metadata identities and recover partial S3/DynamoDB completion. Scheduler execution permission and failed-delivery retries are separate from handler business success. Configure explicit timezone/window requirements.
Sandbox evidence

Walkthroughs are illustrative and should be executed only in a disposable authorized account. Capture event/request IDs, expected outcomes and redacted evidence; verify negative tests and remove sandbox-only rules, identities, queues, logs and releases after use.

title: API product features, payloads and timeouts
rows: REST versus HTTP API

REST has supported request validation/body transformations, usage plans/API keys, cache, canary releases, resource policies, WAF and private API endpoints. HTTP API is a leaner RESTful product with compatible JWT/IAM/Lambda auth and auto deployments. Both can support mTLS; verify configuration.
Private backend support

Current REST VPC links V2 can integrate with supported ALB/NLB backends; V1 is legacy. HTTP API private integrations have their own ALB/NLB/Cloud Map options. REST private Cloud Map integration is not supported. Private backend access does not make the API endpoint private.
Buffered REST payload/time

Payload 10 MB. Usual integration timeout 50ms–29s; Regional/private REST can request greater timeouts, potentially reducing regional account throttle. Edge-optimized buffered timeout cannot be increased through that ordinary limit. Lambda 6 MB buffered payload may constrain the chain earlier.
HTTP API limits

Payload 10 MB; integration timeout maximum 30 seconds, not increasable. These limits are distinct from REST response streaming and Lambda timeout. Default stages 10 and routes 300 are quota entries, not unlimited resources.
REST response streaming

Supported HTTP_PROXY/AWS_PROXY response-transfer STREAM mode works on REST endpoint types, up to 15 minutes and beyond the ordinary 10 MB response boundary. No request streaming. Endpoint cache, response VTL transformation and content encoding are not supported in STREAM mode; compress in the integration if appropriate.
Streaming idle/bandwidth gates

REST stream idle timeouts:5 minutes Regional/private and 30 seconds edge-optimized; customer CloudFront response timeout is a separate setting. API stream first 10 MB is uncapped, then 2 MB/s; Lambda stream has a separate 6 MB threshold. A disconnected client does not necessarily stop Lambda execution.
Regional rate quota

Typical account/Region shared quota across REST, HTTP, WebSocket and callbacks:10,000 RPS with 5,000burst bucket. Some Regions default 2,500/1,250. Actual assigned quotas and downstream rates govern capacity; burst is service-determined, not freely customer-configured.
Stages, deployments and imports

REST stage points to an API deployment; deployment and rollback preserve configuration history, not all data/side effects. Stage default quota 10, increasable where supported. HTTP auto-deploy support differs; OpenAPI definition import does not supply target permissions or network setup.
Large-object upload

Presign only after trusted identity/tenant authorization. Scope key, method, expiry, headers and supported size/checksum conditions; clients upload directly to S3. Enforce CORS where required and verify completion/encryption. URL disclosure grants its supported bearer capability.
ALB Lambda target limits

Same account/Region for function and target group; one function per target group. Request body 1 MB and response JSON1 MB. No WebSocket upgrades on Lambda targets. ALB invokes Lambda directly, so an imagined ALB-SG outbound TCP connection to the function is not the permission model.
Function URL permissions

For new URLs since October 2025, both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions are required. AWS_IAM uses SigV4; NONE still needs an appropriate function resource policy and is public unauthenticated access. Cross-account policy requirements and InvokedViaFunctionUrl restrictions matter.

title: API authorization, browser behavior and cache details
rows: REST policy context

Evaluate caller IAM/method authorization and supported API resource policy together. IP/CIDR, principal and VPC/endpoint conditions have distinct meaning; explicit deny still applies. Backend integration role/Lambda resource permissions are another gate.
IAM, Cognito and custom tokens

AWS_IAM uses signed requests. REST Cognito authorizers validate compatible user-pool tokens; HTTP JWT authorizers validate supported issuer/audience/time/scope rules. Lambda authorizers implement a supported custom contract; a raw SAML assertion is not automatically a JWT accepted by every authorizer.
Authorizer caching

A cached policy/decision must be scoped to relevant identity sources, routes and authorization context. Test revoked/changed access, tenant identity and policy resource patterns; cached authentication must not widen data permissions.
CORS semantics

CORS is enforced by browsers and is not API authentication. Configure preflight OPTIONS and actual/error-response headers. Credentialed requests require compatible explicit origin/credentials settings; wildcard origin does not authorize credentialed access. Backend side effects can happen even when the browser rejects response access.
API keys and plans

Keys identify metered consumers; protect APIs with IAM/Cognito/authorizers. Plan rate/quota targets aggregate across associated stages; a key is associated with only one plan per stage. Best-effort throttles/quotas can be exceeded and are not hard spending caps.
REST cache sizing and TTL

Supported cacheClusterSize choices include 0.5,1.6,6.1,13.5,28.4,58.2,118 and 237 GB; verify current API values. TTL default 300s, configurable 0–3600; zero disables. Maximum cached response 1,048,576bytes; encryption can increase its stored size. Cache provisioning/resizing can take minutes and resizing clears data.
Method and key behavior

When default stage method caching is enabled, GET methods cache by default; override explicitly for other methods. Include required tenant/resource/variant inputs in cache keys and preserve authorization before serving sensitive content. Monitor CacheHitCount/CacheMissCount.
Invalidation controls

A supported Cache-Control:max-age=0 request can invalidate an entry with appropriate permissions/policy; do not assume any anonymous client can flush data. Whole-stage flush, per-method settings and cache encryption are distinct. Cached stale responses need bounded freshness expectations.
TLS and DNS

Use supported custom-domain mappings and certificate ownership/validation. Edge-optimized API custom-domain certificates require us-east-1; Regional certificates use the API Region. Choose supported DNS alias/CNAME records rather than treating a service hostname as an A-record IP.
Private API gates

Private REST access uses execute-api interface endpoints with DNS/security-group reachability plus endpoint/resource/method policies. aws:SourceVpc/SourceVpce can restrict context. A supported connected on-premises network can reach the private path; it is not limited to a client physically inside one subnet.

title: API evidence, errors and WebSocket lifecycle
rows: Error interpretation

400input;401/403auth/policy/path/WAF possibilities;429throttle evidence;502integration/response contract;503unavailability;504integrationtimeout. Use access/integration logs and backend request IDs; do not assert all 502s mean out-of-order invocation.
Logs and metrics by product

REST supports stage execution logs, access logs, detailed metrics, cache metrics, supported Firehose access-log delivery and X-Ray tracing. HTTP supports metrics/access logs but not the full REST execution-log/X-Ray/cache set. Avoid logging tokens and personal data.
Latency interpretation

Latency and IntegrationLatency have different scope. Compare gateway overhead, authorizer latency, initialization and backend duration. Increasing function memory is not a generic fix for policy denial, network egress failure or malformed proxy output.
WebSocket routes and state

Use$connect,$disconnect,$default and message-content-selected custom routes. Persist trusted connection/user/tenant associations where needed. Authentication at connection establishment does not authorize every later data operation automatically.
WebSocket limits

Connection maximum 2 hours; idle timeout 10 minutes; frame 32 KB; message 128 KB requiring compliant framing. Integration timeout 50ms–29s. Typical new connection default 500/s per account/Region, subject to increase. No explicit concurrent-connection quota does not mean unlimited practical capacity.
Management callback

Use signed HTTPS POST to correct /stage/@connections/{connectionId} management endpoint; client connects through wss. Backend needs scoped execute-api:ManageConnections. Custom domains can change stage/path construction. GoneException can mean stale or not-yet-established connection.
Disconnect/recovery

Handle client reconnect, connection-state cleanup and missed updates. Best-effort disconnect delivery cannot be the only cleanup mechanism. Retained database connection records do not make a network socket durable.

title: AppSync schema, identity and real-time boundaries
rows: Schema and resolver responsibility

GraphQL schema specifies fields/types/operations; resolvers implement data access. Supported DynamoDB, eligible Aurora/Data API, OpenSearch, HTTP and Lambda adapters each have their own compatibility, mapping, role and network requirements.
Authorization choices

API_KEY,AWS_IAM,OPENID_CONNECT,AMAZON_COGNITO_USER_POOLS and AWS_LAMBDA modes are supported for GraphQL with configuration restrictions. API key is for a suitable unauthenticated/public API contract, not trusted private user identity. Additional modes require deliberate field/type rules.
Cognito group versus item authorization

Group claims can allow reader queries and restrict writer mutations. Resolver/application owner/tenant conditions and scoped backend IAM are still required. Test forbidden fields, cross-tenant item keys, list predicates and mutations.
Subscriptions

GraphQL subscriptions are mutation-linked secure WebSocket updates with supported filters and authorization. Select fields/payloads correctly and protect cross-tenant subscriptions. Connection establishment does not guarantee every event is retained for replay.
Offline synchronization

Local cache, offline writes, delta/full sync and version/conflict behavior depend on supported client/data-source tooling. A bare GraphQL schema or WebSocket is not a generic offline synchronization implementation; validate reconnect reconciliation.
AppSync Events distinction

Current AppSync Events is a separate managed event publish/subscribe API with its own channel/authorization contract. Do not silently treat GraphQL resolvers/subscriptions and Events as identical. Historic MQTT-over-WebSocket wording is not a universal protocol guarantee.
Observability and efficiency

Use supported AppSync logs/metrics and safe request correlation. Field selection is not proof of fewer backend operations; inspect resolver fan-out, request sizes, datastore capacity, errors and total cost. A successful auth token check does not prove negative tenant tests.

title: Step Functions limits and state contracts
rows: Standard duration
A Standard execution can run up to one year; execution history is durable.
Express duration
An Express execution runs up to five minutes.
Express delivery
Asynchronous Express is at least once; synchronous Express is at most once.
Exactly-once scope
Standard workflow execution does not automatically make an external task side effect exactly once.
State types
Task, Wait, Choice, Parallel, Map, Pass, Succeed and Fail each have distinct transitions.
Optimized integration
Service-specific integration patterns include request/response, .sync and callback where supported.
AWS SDK integration
Supported API action contract and execution-role permissions must be selected explicitly.
Retry
Error match, interval, backoff, maximum attempts and jitter bound retries.
Catch
Catch order and ResultPath determine recovery input after retry exhaustion.
Callback
Task token is sensitive; SendTaskSuccess/Failure, timeout and heartbeat govern resumption.

title: SQS ordering, timing and recovery
rows: Standard queue
At-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering; consumers need idempotency.
FIFO group
Ordering applies within each MessageGroupId; groups can process in parallel.
FIFO deduplication
Five-minute deduplication window does not remove downstream idempotency need.
Message maximum
Current SQS message body maximum is 1 MiB; larger payloads require a separate object/pointer design.
Retention
Configure from one minute to 14 days; default is four days.
Visibility
Default 30 seconds; configurable up to 12 hours; extend for longer work then delete on success.
Long polling
ReceiveMessage wait time can reach 20 seconds to reduce empty responses.
Delay
Queue or per-message delay is bounded at 15 minutes; use Scheduler for longer schedules.
In-flight
Standard approximate in-flight quota and FIFO behavior vary; monitor capacity and delete completed work.
DLQ
Redrive policy and maxReceiveCount isolate poison messages; compatible queue types and permissions matter.
Redrive
Inspect cause and receive count before moving messages back to a source queue.
Lambda partial batch
FunctionResponseTypes ReportBatchItemFailures returns failed message IDs; successful records are deleted.
Backlog signals
ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, NotVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage support alarms.

title: SNS publication, fanout and security
rows: Topic fanout
Publish to a topic; every matching subscription receives independently.
Filter scope
Filter policy can select message attributes or JSON body, with propagation time.
SNS FIFO
FIFO topic ordering by group applies to eligible subscriptions; SNS FIFO can fan out to SQS FIFO or Standard.
FIFO Lambda path
Direct Lambda subscription is not eligible for FIFO topic; bridge via SQS where needed.
Mobile push
Platform application owns platform endpoints; Publish to endpoint TargetArn or subscribe endpoint.
Email
SNS email endpoint delivery is direct from SNS, without an Amazon SES hop.
Large message
Beyond conventional 256 KiB, configurable large messages apply only to eligible Firehose/SQS/Lambda endpoints and subscription count bounds.
Encrypted topic
KMS policy and SNS permissions must allow publishing and delivery; SQS encryption has its own key policy.
SQS queue policy
Grant sns.amazonaws.com sqs:SendMessage scoped to the specific source topic ARN.

title: EventBridge routing and replay
rows: Bus types
Default, custom and partner event buses organize source events.
Pattern
Rules inspect source, detail-type and detail fields; nonmatching events do not invoke targets.
Target failure
Retry/DLQ cover failed target API delivery under policy; downstream handler failure is separate.
Cross-account
Source PutEvents IAM and target bus resource policy both matter; target permissions remain separate.
Archive
Archive selected bus events with filter and retention for later replay.
Replay
Replay re-submits events to a bus and can trigger matching rules again; design idempotency.
Schema registry
Discovery, versioning and generated bindings aid typed consumers; schema evolution remains a contract.
Ordering
An event bus does not provide queue-like per-group ordered delivery.

title: Scheduler, Pipes and broker choices
rows: Scheduler
One-time, rate and cron schedules support time zones and flexible time windows.
Schedule delivery
Execution role, retry policy and SQS DLQ govern target invocation; choose cleanup action.
Pipes stages
Supported source -> optional filtering -> optional enrichment -> target.
Pipes checkpoint
Retries and checkpoint behavior depend on source; execution role needs read/invoke/write access.
Amazon MQ engine
Managed ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ brokers suit compatible protocols; size and operate broker topology.
Migration
IBM MQ and TIBCO are not native drop-in engines; test protocol/client/adapter migration.

title: CloudFront caching and distribution contract
rows: Hit versus miss
A hit returns from an edge cache; a miss forwards via CloudFront origin path. Origin events do not run on a hit.
Cache key
Cache policy includes selected headers, cookies and query strings; the resulting key isolates variants.
Origin request
Origin request policy can forward values without placing them in the cache key.
TTL controls
Min/default/max TTL combine with origin Cache-Control or Expires according to policy.
Stale content
Use versioned URLs or invalidations; inspect cache and origin headers before changing TTL.
Dynamic API
CloudFront can accelerate HTTP APIs without caching sensitive responses by default.
Price classes
All, 200 and 100 change edge coverage; pricing varies by geography and current schedule.
Geo restriction
Country allow/block uses GeoIP and is not user authentication.
Custom error
Error page, status mapping and Error Caching Minimum TTL may alter viewer-visible failure.
Security overlay
AWS Shield, AWS WAF and TLS are separate from cache-key correctness.

title: Origins, OAC and failover
rows: Private S3 REST
Use OAC with distribution-scoped bucket policy and KMS grant for SSE-KMS objects where needed.
OAC versus OAI
OAC is recommended for current S3 origins, KMS and dynamic methods.
S3 website
Website endpoint is custom HTTP origin; OAC/OAI do not apply and origin HTTPS is unsupported.
S3 upload
CloudFront PUT/DELETE to S3 needs OAC and narrow bucket policy; prevent unintended deletion.
ALB origin
An ordinary custom origin endpoint must be reachable; ALB may serve private EC2 targets.
ALB direct access
CloudFront managed prefix list plus secret custom origin header/listener rule can restrict direct requests.
VPC origin
CloudFront supports private ALB, NLB and EC2 in VPC subnets through the VPC origins feature; check restrictions and connectivity separately from public custom origins.
Origin failover
Only GET, HEAD and cached OPTIONS eligible; configured error codes and timeouts determine fallback.
Failover scope
Each request first tries primary; secondary is selected only after qualifying primary failure.
Cross-Region replication
S3 CRR creates regional copies; edge caching serves transient copies with TTL.
Origin response
Status and headers can change caching/failover; test error handling separately.

title: Signed viewer access and policy
rows: Trusted key group
Application signs with private key; CloudFront verifies with associated public key group.
Signed URL
Use for individual object or custom policy with expiry and optional IP or start-time constraints.
Signed cookies
Use when restricting multiple files or leaving URLs unchanged; URL policy can override cookie on same request.
S3 presign
SigV4 signs a specific S3 API request using a principal’s permission; separate from CloudFront signed access.
Viewer versus origin
Signed URL/cookie controls viewer; OAC controls CloudFront-to-S3; configure both for private delivery.
Key rotation
Manage public keys and key groups independently of obsolete root-account key pair guidance.
Direct origin bypass
A public origin can bypass CloudFront signed access; protect origin access as well.
Geo and auth
Country restriction is coarse; validate identity/token claims for user authorization.

title: CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge
rows: Function triggers
CloudFront Functions run only on viewer request or viewer response.
Lambda triggers
Lambda@Edge runs viewer request/response and origin request/response.
Cache hits
Origin request/response Lambda@Edge runs only when request reaches origin.
Shared viewer event
Do not combine CloudFront Function and Lambda@Edge on viewer events for the same cache behavior.
Valid combination
A Function on viewer event may combine with Lambda@Edge on origin event.
Functions runtime
JavaScript runtime; KVS requires runtime 2.0; no network, file system or request body.
Lambda runtime
Supported Node.js/Python versions and published version in us-east-1, replicated by CloudFront.
Function response
Viewer response functions are skipped for origin 4xx/5xx; origin response Lambda sees origin errors.
JWT checks
Validate signature, expiry, issuer/audience and policy; decoding alone is insufficient.
Origin rewrite
Lambda@Edge origin request can select origin on misses; preserve host/DNS and policy correctness.
Quota drift
Execution time, memory, deployment size and pricing can change; use linked AWS quota page.

title: Global Accelerator traffic and endpoints
rows: Anycast
Standard accelerator supplies static entry IPs on the AWS global network to regional endpoints.
Listener
TCP or UDP listener port/range receives client traffic; no HTTP object cache.
Endpoint choices
Standard endpoints include ALB, NLB, EC2 and Elastic IP; custom routing uses subnets.
Health
New connections route based on endpoint health; if none healthy, fallback behavior needs evaluation.
Traffic dial
Percentage applies to traffic already directed to that regional endpoint group.
Endpoint weight
Relative weights distribute traffic among endpoints within group; health can change selection.
Client IP
Preservation support/default depends on endpoint type and configuration.
Inspection caveat
With preserved client IP, certain VPC inspection paths may be bypassed; assess security groups and WAF.
CloudFront difference
Global Accelerator proxies TCP/UDP to applications; CloudFront delivers HTTP(S) with edge caching.
DNS difference
Stable anycast addresses avoid dependence on DNS failover cache timing for entry point.

title: Data Exchange entitlement and delivery
rows: Subscription
Review provider terms, pricing, entitlements and update cadence.
S3 files
Export revisions to a controlled S3 bucket and plan storage, encryption and access.
API or tables
Delivery contracts vary by product; use the provider-supported entitlement and consumption method.
Governance
Catalog and grant lake access separately from subscription permissions.

title: Kinesis Data Streams capacity and consumers
rows: Partition key
Maps records to shards; the same key preserves per-shard order but can create a hot shard.
Retention
Default retention can be extended; retained records permit consumer replay within the configured window.
Provisioned
Select shard capacity and reshard as demand changes.
On-demand
The service adjusts stream capacity; review current mode-specific limits and regional quotas.
Standard polling
Consumers share read throughput per shard.
Enhanced fan-out
Registered consumers receive dedicated read throughput per shard.
Checkpoint
KCL and Lambda event source mappings track progress; retries can cause duplicate processing.
Monitoring
Watch write throttling, iterator age, consumer lag and hot keys.

rows: Firehose buffer
Size or time hint can trigger delivery; destination and partitioning settings affect latency.
Transformation
Lambda can return processed, dropped or processing-failed outcomes per record.
Backup
Configure S3 backup and error prefixes; inspect and replay failures deliberately.
Redshift
Firehose stages in S3 before COPY into Redshift.
Flink state
Event-time windows, joins and state require checkpoint and restore design.
External sinks
Exactly-once state does not automatically guarantee exactly-once external side effects.

title: MSK Kafka and Batch job placement
rows: MSK topic
Partitions define per-partition order and consumer-group parallelism.
MSK clients
Kafka protocol, offsets, replication and poison-message handling remain application concerns.
Batch queue
RUNNABLE jobs await eligible capacity and matching job constraints.
Compute environment
Choose managed or unmanaged compute with compatible EC2, Fargate or eligible alternatives.
Multi-node
Coordinated main/child nodes require eligible EC2 capacity; no Fargate or Spot.
Private networking
Container image pulls, logs and data paths need routes or service endpoints.
